sec.title: Background
sec.p: Honey exhibits a broad spectrum of antibacterial activity against Gram‐positive and Gram‐negative bacteria, including methicillin‐resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) ones. Chitosan (Cs) is a mucoadhesive polymer that also has antibacterial properties. Special attention has been paid to the design of polymeric nanoparticles (NPs) as new nano drug delivery systems to overcome bacterial resistance and its problems.

sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: The aim of the present study is to synthesize Cs‐meropenem NPs with/without honey as an antibiofilm and antibacterial agent to inhibit Staphylococcus aureus.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This study synthesized meropenem and honey‐loaded Cs nanogels and subsequently characterized them by Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM), Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), and DLS‐zeta potential. Using the broth microdilution and crystal violet assays, the antibacterial and antibiofilm activity of meropenem and honey‐loaded Cs nanogel, free meropenem, free honey, and free Cs NPs were investigated in vitro against MRSA strains. 3‐(4,5‐dimethylthiazol‐2‐yl)‐2,5‐diphenyl‐2H‐tetrazolium bromide (MTT) was also used to test the cytotoxicity of several Cs‐NPs compound against the HEK‐293 regular cell line.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The average size of meropenem and honey‐Cs‐NPs was reported to be 119.885 nm, and encapsulation efficiency was 88.33 ± 0.97 with stability up to 60 days at 4°C. The NPs showed enhanced antibiofilm efficacy against S. aureus at sub‐minimum inhibitory concentrations. Additionally, the cytotoxicity of meropenem and honey‐encapsulated Cs against the HEK‐293 normal cell line was insignificant.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our findings suggested that meropenem and honey‐Cs‐NPs might be potential antibacterial and antibiofilm materials.

abstract.p: The subject of my article is the synthesis of chitosan nanoparticles in conjunction with the utilization of mupirocin and honey. Our aim was to examine the combined effect of these three substances on combating methicillin‐resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), a strain known for its resistance to conventional treatments. Until now, the combined impact of these three substances had not been thoroughly investigated. Given the urgent issue of antibiotic resistance in today's world, the significance of utilizing nanoparticles and materials with antibacterial and antioxidant properties cannot be overstated.

The results of our research demonstrate that the simultaneous use of chitosan, honey, and mupirocin produces superior outcomes compared to the use of mupirocin and honey alone. It appears that this combination could serve as an effective solution in addressing MRSA infections resistant to treatment.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Antibiotic‐resistant bacterial strains have become a significant public health concern across the world. Each year, several million people become infected with antibiotic‐resistant bacteria, with at least 25,000 people dying directly from these illnesses (Balaure et al., 2017). Staphylococcus aureus is a common human pathogen that causes various infections in the community and hospitals, including infective endocarditis, bloodstream, bone, skin, and soft tissue infections (Abd El‐Baky et al., 2019). One of the most significant issues that leads to therapeutic failure is S. aureus resistance to antimicrobial drugs. Antibiotic resistance has emerged due to the extensive use and misuse of antimicrobials for treating many infectious illnesses in humans and animals. This resistance might be due to one or more antibiotic classes. Furthermore, among isolated strains, the emergence of diverse resistance patterns such as multidrug resistance (MDR), extensively drug‐resistant (EDR), and pan‐drug resistance has become widespread (Khan et al., 2020). The difficulty and failure of staphylococcal infection treatments are due to the presence of several antibiotic resistance mechanisms, including their ability to form a biofilm, enzymatic degradation of antimicrobials, modification of the target site, and reduction of the intracellular concentration of antibiotics by efflux mechanisms (Kumar & Schweizer, 2005).

Treating S. aureus infections is challenging due to several reasons (Kashef et al., 2020). Staphylococcus aureus has developed resistance to a wide range of medicines (Kashef et al., 2020). A report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention classified methicillin‐resistant S. aureus (MRSA) as a “severe hazard,” with 323,700 instances of invasive MRSA infections and around 10,600 fatalities documented between 2012 and 2017 (CDC A, 2019). MRSA is resistant to all presently available beta‐lactam antibiotics, as well as to the majority of non‐beta‐lactam antibiotics. Meropenem and vancomycin are the most often prescribed antibiotics in treating infections caused by methicillin‐resistant strains of S. aureus (MRSA) (Shadvar et al., 2021). Meropenem (also known as Merrem) is a broad‐spectrum antibiotic usually prescribed as a strategic drug to treat systemic bacterial infections such as pneumonia, meningitis, sepsis, and anthrax (Fish, 2006). According to the earlier study, meropenem, while taken with other antibiotics, boosts its effectiveness against MRSA strains (Gonzales et al., 2015). However, abuse of meropenem during the last year has led to a rise in the number of enterococci with the meropenem resistance gene. There is a significant risk of plasmids with resistance genes migrating to S. aureus strains via conjugation (Elshamy & Aboshanab, 2020). As a result, S. aureus strains with lower sensitivity to meropenem have developed, posing a danger to the drug's future usage. Another challenge for antibiotic resistance in S. aureus strains is biofilm development, which has become a significant concern in hospital‐acquired infections (Khatoon et al., 2018). DNA, polysaccharides, and proteins constitute a biofilm or glycocalyx. Bacteria are packed firmly in an extracellular polysaccharide matrix, which helps them evade the immune system and antimicrobials in the environment. Many antibiotics cannot penetrate this matrix, resulting in a considerable reduction in antimicrobial effectiveness. Due to restricted nutritional supply, bacterial cells in deep layers of biofilm have a poor rate of metabolism and development (Franco, 2017). So, developing new antimicrobials against S. aureus infection is desperately needed. This is addressed by the challenges that face the drug development process, such as the considerable time spent generating novel drugs with a low success rate and unknown safety (Livermore, 2011). Enhancing the effectiveness of current medications is an alternative to drug discovery and development. Advances in nanotechnology have recently presented a promising approach to improving the activity and safety of existing antibacterial drugs. Antimicrobial formulations in nano forms and other vesicular systems significantly improve efficacy and selective delivery to extracellular and intracellular infections, as well as antibiofilm activities, compared to free drug formulations (Ahmed et al., 2019, Pourmoghadasiyan et al., 2022). Nanomedicines serve as drug delivery devices that enable the extended circulation of pharmaceuticals while preserving their biological efficacy. Furthermore, they mitigate the adverse reactions of medications and specifically focus on targeted cells (Amale et al., 2021).

Besides nutritional value, honey has been therapeutic since ancient times. This traditional remedy's antibacterial activity was first discovered in the 20th century (Allen et al., 1991). Many researchers have focused on honey's broad antibacterial efficacy against infections, oral pathogens, and food‐borne germs (Khalili Samani et al., 2021). Honey's efficacy in vitro against multidrug‐resistant (MDR) bacteria and its ability to treat infected wounds has rekindled interest in honey as an antibacterial agent (Sobhani et al., 2017). It was shown to have significant antibacterial action compared to routinely utilized antimicrobial agents (Khalili Samani et al., 2021).

Antimicrobial biomaterials based on polymers or polymer composites have been discovered due to the ongoing quest for possible antimicrobial agents (Sobhani et al., 2017). Chitosan (Cs) is one example of them. It (poly B‐(1‐4)‐2‐amino‐2‐deoxy‐d‐glucose) has high antimicrobial activity as a polycationic biopolymer (Gómez‐Burgaz et al., 2009). Non‐toxicity, biodegradability, low price, good biocompatibility, and non‐antigenicity are all benefits of this natural polysaccharide (Rao et al., 2012). The theorized mechanism for its antimicrobial effect is that it binds to the negatively charged bacterial cell wall, causing instability of the cell envelope and reduced permeability, and then attaches to DNA, preventing it from replicating (Xing et al., 2009). In light of these considerations, antibacterial drugs’ efficacy against pathogens can be improved by loading them inside Cs‐nanoparticles (NPs). The therapeutic efficiency of the nanoparticulate drug delivery system may be improved by raising the antibiotic concentration in the microorganism without increasing the antibiotic dosage administered (Azhdarzadeh et al., 2012). In the present work, we developed meropenem and honey‐loaded Cs‐NPs as a potent antimicrobial agent against multiresistant S. aureus strains to reduce antibiotic resistance and increase antimicrobial effects.

sec.title: Materials
sec.p: Low molecular weight Cs and N‐(3‐dimethylaminopropyl)‐N′‐ethyl carbodiimide hydrochloride (EDC) were purchased from Sigma Aldrich Co. Tryptic soy broth culture was purchased from Merck Co. Exira Pharmaceutical Co. provided the meropenem (Merrem). Blood agar base, Muller Hinton agar culture, and congo red dye were purchased from Merck Co. Natural Khansar honey was prepared from Sharekord.

sec.title: Preparation of different formulations of Cs NPs
sec.p: Briefly, 1 g of Cs powder at 100 mL distilled water containing hydrogen chloride was solved using the magnetic stirrer. Afterwards, the solution was centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 5 min. Then, 50 mg myristic acid, 100 mg EDC, and N‐hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) were solved in 1 mL ethanol (myristic solution 2). The solution was then dropped into the Cs solution while being vigorously magnetically stirred at room temperature. Finally, the reaction pH increased with diluted NaOH, and CHs NPs were harvested after centrifugation (Wang & Luo, 2018). Meropenem and honey Cs‐NPs were synthesized in different combinations, which are listed in Table 1.

sec.title: NPs characterization
sec.p: Using dynamic light scattering (DLS) and ZetaPlas palladium electrodes, the average size, size distribution, and zeta potential of meropenem‐honey loaded in Cs were measured. To avoid repeated scattering due to particle interactions, the freshly generated Cs combinations were diluted two times with distilled water at a 20:1 ratio, and analysis was performed at 25°C with a 90° light scattering angle. The average z diameter and multiple scattering index of Cs‐NPs and their zeta potentials were calculated. To create electrical conductivity, Cs‐encapsulated meropenem and honey particles were coated with a gold layer and studied using a Field‐Emission Scanning Electron Microscopes equipment model MIRA3 (TESCAN) and Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) device model X ‘Pert Pro (Haghighi et al., 2020).

sec.title: Efficacy of drug encapsulation
sec.p:
The encapsulation efficiency was assessed using the method described by Cevher et al. (2006). NPs were isolated from the suspension by ultracentrifugation at 10,000 g and 4°C for 30 min after drug loading. A UV‐Vis spectrophotometer set to 270 nm was used to determine the quantity of free meropenem and honey in the supernatant. The encapsulation efficiency (EE) was determined using Equation (1):
(1) EE%=(T−F)T×100, where F denotes the quantity of drug that is free in the supernatant and T denotes the total amount of drug. A blank sample was created using Khosravi et al. (2020).

sec.title: In vitro drug release
sec.p: In phosphate buffer solution, a comparative in vitro drug release investigation was carried out at three various pH values of 3.0, 5.0, and 7.4. Drug‐loaded Cs‐NPs were soaked in 5.0 mL phosphate‐buffered saline (PBS), placed in the dialysis membrane (cutoff: 12 kDa, MWCO, supplier: Kimia Teb Tajhiz), tied at both ends, and submerged in the cell containing 100 mL of PBS. The cell was placed in a shaker incubator (Farazma) at 37°C and 25 rpm. To estimate the drug concentration in the receiving compartment, samples (5 mL) were taken from the cell at regular intervals and replaced with the same volume of fresh pre‐warmed PBS solution to avoid saturation phenomena and preserve the sink condition. At 270 nm, the samples were evaluated. The released dose at each time point was determined and shown on a cumulative release curve (Mehrabi et al., 2021).

sec.title: Isolation of bacterial strain
sec.p: Staphylococcus aureus isolation was done from 300 patients (175 women and 125 men, average age 42 years) referring to the Hajar Hospital (Iran, Shahrekord—Nurse St.), Kashani Hospital (Ayatollah Kashani Hospital, Nurse St., Shahrekord), and Emam Ali Hospital (Shahrekord—7 km of Shahrekord Road—Farrokhshahr) in Sharekord during the period from 2021 to 2022. Patients with clinical symptoms such as fever, chills and sweating were treated with antibiotics ciprofloxacin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol, amikacin, tetracycline, imipenem, tazobactam, ampicillin, sulbactam, kanamycin and ceftazidime. After 15 days of treatment with different antibiotics, urine sample was collected from patients who had not improved their symptoms.

sec.title: Sampling, culture, and diagnosis of S. aureus isolates
sec.p: Using sterile swabs, the collected isolates from urine samples were cultured in blood agar, Tryptic Soy Broth (TSB), MacConkey agar, and Simmons citrate agar cultures at 37°C for 24 h. Gram staining, catalase, oxidase, urease, and lysine decarboxylase assays confirmed the presence of S. aureus isolates. For subsequent studies, S. aureus was cultured in 30% glycerol and kept at −80°C.

sec.title: Antimicrobial sensitivity
sec.p: After S. aureus strains were identified and verified, the sensitivity of the strains to various antibiotics was tested using the disk diffusion method based on the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI, 2019) protocol. Staphylococcus aureus isolates sensitivity to imipenem (IMI, 10 µg), methicillin (MET, 10 µg), ciprofloxacin (CIP, 5 µg), vancomycin (VA, 10 µg), erythromycin (E, 15 µg), chloramphenicol (C, 30 µg), amikacin (AK, 10 µg), tetracycline (TE, 30 µg), clindamycin (CD, 2 µg), kanamycin (KAN, 30 µg), ceftazidime (CAZ, 30 µg), and colistin (CS, 5 µg) (MAST) disks were evaluated in Muller Hinton agar culture. Staphylococcus aureus ATCCBAA 33592, Pseudomonas ATCC 27853, and Acinetobacter ATCC 17978 are considered positive control (CLSI 2020).

sec.title: Biofilm formation detection
sec.p:
The detection of biofilm formation was carried out using the method of Mariana et al. Briefly, an overnight bacterial culture was grown at 37°C in Congo red agar plate supplemented with glucose (50 g/L), agar (10 g/L), congo red (0.08%), and BHIA with sucrose (37 g/L). The capacity of isolates to produce biofilms was determined using a plate microtiter test. Through this assay, emptying the wells and washing them with PBS solution, 1% violet crystal was used to stain them. Afterwards, each well was filled with 10% sample and 70% ethanol. The light absorbance was measured using an ELISA Reader Stat Fax2100 (Awareness Technology) at a wavelength of 570 nm (Mariana et al., 2009). The findings of biofilm development were divided into four categories:
Non‐biofilm producer: OD≤ODc
Weak biofilm producer: ODc<OD≤2*ODc
Moderate biofilm producer: 2*ODc<OD≤4*ODc
Strong biofilm producer: 4*ODc<OD

sec.title: Assays for the antibiofilm activity of meropenem‐honey Cs NPs
Determination of minimum inhibitory concentration and minimum bactericidal concentration
sec.p: Various Cs‐encapsulated meropenem and honey combinations were investigated for antibacterial efficacy against multiresistant S. aureus strains using broth microdilution. Following that, the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) were measured. After culturing S. aureus for 24 h in Müller Hinton broth, 51 × 105 CFU/mL bacteria, 100 µL of various Cs‐encapsulated meropenem combinations, Cs‐encapsulated honey, Cs‐encapsulated meropenem, honey, free meropenem, and free Cs (in concentrations ranging from 0.03 to 64 µg/L) were poured into each well of a 96‐well plate and incubated for 24 h. The sub‐MIC values of the positive control well (containing culture medium plus standard S. aureus strain ATCC 33592), negative control well (containing pure culture medium), and negative control well (containing culture medium plus standard S. aureus strain ATCC 33592) were determined, and the test was replicated (Piri‐Gharaghie et al., 2022; Qi et al., 2004).

sec.title: Antibiofilm activity
sec.p: Minimum biofilm inhibition concentration (MBIC) was determined using sub‐MIC concentrations of free meropenem and Cs, as well as different combinations of Cs‐encapsulated meropenem, against the four S. aureus strains that make up the biofilm (Sample 7, Sample 12, Sample 15, and Sample 31) and standard S. aureus ATCC 33592. The 96‐well plate was filled with a 100‐µL drug sample and a 100‐µL culture of bacteria in Müller Hinton broth. After being washed, the plates were incubated for 48 h at 37°C under static conditions and stained with violet crystal. The tests were repeated twice, and the average MBIC was found to be 570 nm (Tan et al., 2018).

sec.title: Evaluation of biofilm gene expression
sec.p: Using the specific primers listed in Table 2, the expressions of the biofilm genes OmpA, Bap, and pgaB were investigated by Quantitative Real Time‐PCR (qRT‐PCR). After 24 h of being exposed to sub‐MIC quantities of free meropenem, Cs, honey, Cs‐encapsulated meropenem, Cs‐encapsulated honey, and Cs‐encapsulated meropenem and honey, RNA was extracted from multiresistant S. aureus bacteria using the RNX‐Plus kit (CinnaGen), and cDNA was generated using the RNA extracted according to the YTA Kit methodology (Yekta Tajhiz). A real‐time PCR instrument type Corbett 5 Plex HRM was used to analyze biofilm gene expression compared to the 16SrRNA gene (as the reference gene; Corbett). The final reaction volume was 15 µL, with 1 µL of cDNA, 1 µL of forward primer, 1 µL of reverse primer, 8 µL of master mix, and 4 µL of deionized water (Merck). The temperature cycle included an initial denaturation for 5 min at 95°C, followed by 40 cycles of 20 seconds at 95°C, 40 seconds at 58°C, and 40 seconds at 72°C. To draw melting curves, the last stage was set to 53–95°C. The Ct technique was used to investigate the quantitative relative expression of genes (Piri‐Gharaghie et al., 2022).

sec.title: Cytotoxicity study
sec.p:
Note that 5‐2 × 104 cells derived from the human embryonic kidney (HEK 293) cell line were seeded into each well of a 96‐well plate in supplemented RPMI‐1640 complete medium (containing penicillin‐streptomycin 10000 U/ml and fetal bovine serum 10%) and incubated for 24 h at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2 before being assessed with the colorimetric MTT ((3‐(4, 5‐dimethylthiazol‐2‐yl)‐2, 5‐ diphenyl‐tetrazolium bromide) dye. The samples were then added to each well at various concentrations ranging from 0.125 to 256 µL/mL and incubated for another 24 h. Afterwards, each well was filled with 100 µL of 0.5 mg/mL MTT and incubated for 3 h. After removing the culture media, 20 min of dimethyl sulfoxide was applied to dissolve the sediment that had developed at the bottom of each well. Finally, the absorbance of each well was determined at 570 nm using a microplate reader (Li et al., 2015; Riss et al., 2004). The following equation was used to calculate cell viability:
(2) Cellviability%=OD570sample/OD570control×100.

sec.title: Animals and their care
sec.p: At the Department of Biotechnology and Molecular Biology's animal house facility, female BALB/c mice were produced and maintained at a constant room temperature of 25 ± 2°C and humidity of 40%–70%. The mice were kept in plastic cages with hardwood chips as bedding and in polypropylene cages with a natural 12‐h day/night cycle. The mice were fed a conventional laboratory pellet diet and had unlimited access to water (Shakil et al., 2020). In this experiment, 42 adult female BALB/C mice (weight 20–25 grams and aged 6–8 weeks) were used. For the examination of various formulations of Cs NPs, the mice were infected with 300 µL of S. aureus intraperitoneally (107 CFU/mL) twice 2 weeks in between to induce chronic MRSA infection. After induced chronic infection, the animals were randomly divided into seven groups (six mice/cage). The uninfected group was kept as a positive control and was given 300 µL (0.3 mL) of distilled water, while the other groups were given 0.3 mL of various NPs combinations (C1–C6) for 3 days and every 8 h. The NPs dose was chosen based on the MBIC concentration in each combination. To evaluate treatments, survival was observed for 48 h. At different time intervals (days 7, 14, and 21 after gavage), healthy and dead mice were examined. Compared to the control mice, the animals were tested for changes in fur, body weight, and survival rate after treatment with different combinations of NPs (Hassanen & Ragab, 2021). The mice were observed for a duration of 48 days, during which time the body weight, clinical score, and survival rate of each group were documented. The overall clinical sign of each mouse was assessed using a sliding scale ranging from 0 to −5. The individual clinical ratings were as follows: 0 (indicating normalcy, activity, and health), −1 (indicating slight illness, slight fur ruffling, and otherwise normal condition), −2 (indicating illness, ruffled fur, sluggish movement, and hunching), −3 (indicating extreme illness, ruffled hair, stooped posture, and closed eyes), and −4 (indicating moribund condition).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The data were statistically analyzed using the GraphPad Prism 5.0 program, and each result was represented as mean ± SD. One‐way analysis of variance was used to examine the data. T‐test analysis with p < 0.05 was used to conduct pairwise comparisons of groups. Statistical significance was defined as a value of p < 0.05

sec.title: Characterization of NPs
sec.p: The surface appearance and morphological features of NPs are shown in Figure 1. Cs encapsulated with meropenem and honey NPs were found to have a completely spherical shape and a smooth surface (Figure 1). Two essential characteristics in drug delivery are particle size distribution and zeta potential. The particle size of NPs was validated by DLS and Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM). Table 3 summarizes the physical characterization of the NPs, including size, zeta potential, polydispersity index (PDI), and the efficacy of drug encapsulation. The average particle size of meropenem and honey‐encapsulated Cs‐NPs is 119.885 nm, with a zeta potential of +48.0 ± 1 mV, showing NP stability and a solid electric surface charge on antibiotic‐loaded Cs‐NPs (Table 3). The PDI for meropenem‐Cs, honey‐Cs, and meropenem‐honey‐Cs was less than 0.3, indicating that the NPs had a uniform particle size distribution. As a result, the encapsulation of meropenem and honey in Cs‐NPs lowers porosity, increasing particle size average dispersity.

sec.title: FTIR analysis
sec.p: The presence of components that might be responsible for their synthesis or stabilization was determined using FTIR analysis. The FTIR spectra of meropenem, meropenem‐Cs, meropenem‐honey, honey‐Cs, and meropenem‐honey‐Cs shown in Figure S1 and Table 4 reveal that alterations in some of the individual signals have resulted in the synthesis of meropenem‐honey Cs‐NPs. The functional groups present in the meropenem‐honey (Figure S1C) NPs were compared to their bulk counterparts; meropenem (Figure S1A) showed characteristic peaks at 3334.89 and 1763.84 cm−1, indicating the O–H stretching and carboxyl group, respectively. FTIR spectra of meropenem‐honey Cs reveal a peak at 3398.74 cm−1, as well as four unequal stretching vibrations at 1563.46, 1414.39, 1058.55, and 584.37 cm−1, were assigned to –OH, C–H, –O–C = O, –CH and NH2, respectively (Figure S1E). Meropenem Cs‐NPs exhibited distinctive bands at 3400.39, 1569.68, 1414.01, 1059.44 cm−1, showing O–H, NH2, C–O–C stretching vibration and respectively (Figure S1B). Cs‐meropenem and Cs‐honey characteristic peaks are similar (Figure S1C,D). The C–H bending vibrations are responsible for the peak at 1563 cm−1, whereas the O–H stretching vibrations at the Cs surface are responsible for the broad peak of about 3398.74 cm−1. The appearance of these peaks in the spectrum of meropenem‐honey‐Cs‐NPs confirms the binding relationship between Cs and meropenem and honey via amide bonds. This suggests a chemical reaction between the Cs and the treatment NPs. However, further trials are required for effective field applications.

sec.title: Meropenem and honey‐loaded Cs‐NPs: Loading efficiency and release kinetics
sec.p: The goal of this section is to see how Cs affected drug encapsulation as well as the behavior of meropenem and honey release. The profile of drug release was investigated using dialysis bags containing free meropenem and honey and Cs‐loaded meropenem and honey NPs. Figure 2B shows the results, and meropenem and honey were reported to be loaded onto Cs‐NPs in a quantity of 88.33 ± 0.97%. At 37°C, the in vitro drug release profile of meropenem and honey from Cs‐NPs was determined in a release medium made up of PBS. The pH of the media was adjusted to 3, 5, and 7.4 since the ionic strength of the media is important for the stability and release of the drugs. The release of meropenem and honey from Cs‐NPs showed a biphasic release pattern (Figure 2A). The release kinetics of loaded NPs first showed an explosive release at 6 h, which was followed by a steady and stable release from 12 h onwards. Figure 2A shows the cumulative meropenem and honey release as a function of time. As shown in the figure, the release profile was two‐stage, and in the first stage, the rapid release of meropenem and honey from Cs‐NPs was observed at the rate of 38% in the first 6 h. In the second stage, the release of the drug (meropenem and honey) from Cs NPs is slow, and the remaining drug is released by 60% within 120 h. In the first hour, 82% and 72% of the meropenem and meropenem + honey showed an initial burst release phase. The drug kinetics was gentle afterwards.

sec.title: Screening of resistant bacteria collected from sources
sec.p: After microbiological diagnostic testing, 106 of the 300 collected samples were proven to have methicillin resistance S. aureus. In terms of S. aureus infection, Kashani Hospital had the highest frequency of 45 patients (42.45%), Emam Ali Hospital had 34 patients (32.07%), and Hajar Hospital had the lowest frequency of 27 patients (25.47%) based on the number of samples taken from the hospitals under study (Table 5). Following that, the susceptibility of S. aureus isolates to different antibiotics was investigated, revealing that 93 (87.73%) of the 106 samples were MDR. The findings of the vancomycin screen agar revealed that among 93 MDR isolates, 66 isolates (70.96%) were vancomycin‐resistant. Furthermore, 93 samples (100%) of the 93 MDR isolates were capable of producing biofilms, with the highest frequency seen in Kashani, Hajar, and Emam Ali Hospitals, with 39 (86.6%), 24 (88.8%), and 30 (88.23%) isolates, respectively.

sec.title: Antimicrobial susceptibility and biofilm formation of collected S. aureus isolates
sec.p: One hundred and six (35.33%) of the isolates had the MRSA phenotype, whereas 93 (87.73%) were MDR isolates. Vancomycin resistance was found in 66 (70.96%) of the isolates collected (Table 5). Antibiotic sensitivity testing was done, and the results are listed in Table 6. MDR was assigned to all four isolates that were resistant to three or more antibiotic classes. Biofilm formation was found in all MDR strains, and there was a link between MDR and biofilm formation. The four isolates of Samples 7, 12, 15, and 31, as well as the control S. aureus ATCC 33592 isolate, were chosen as biofilm‐generating strains among the bacterial strains studied. Biofilm‐forming capacity of isolated strains from sources using TSB medium on polystyrene microtiter plate showed strong biofilm formation (Figure 3).

sec.title: Antibacterial and antibiofilm activity of meropenem‐honey Cs NPs
sec.p: The MIC, MBC, and MBIC of free meropenem; free Cs; and various combinations of Cs‐encapsulated meropenem were tested against four selected samples of S. aureus (Table 7). The MIC values of free meropenem, free Cs, and free honey ranged from 2 to 8 µg/mL, and the strains above showed different resistance levels. Furthermore, MBC values did not differ significantly from MIC values. Blank meropenem, Cs, and honey at the concentrations tested failed to suppress biofilm development or eradicate existing biofilms. The antibiofilm activity of Cs‐encapsulated meropenem compared to free meropenem was also investigated using MBIC. Compared to free meropenem, the C6 combination significantly reduced the quantity of biofilm by 28 times the MBIC in all of the samples studied. Blank meropenem, on the other hand, had no fatal impact or growth inhibition at any of the concentrations tested.

sec.title: Cs combination's antibiofilm activity
sec.p: Because biofilm is a common cause of antimicrobial resistance, accounting for 65%−80% of all infections, the synthesized Cs‐NPs were assessed for their efficiency against biofilm formation of isolated MDR samples. To measure the antibiotic activity of different combinations, the MBIC concentration of each strain was used according to Table 7. Figure 4 shows that the biofilm development of the C1 (S. aureus with Cs‐NPs) and C6 (Cs‐encapsulated meropenem with honey) treatments differed significantly. Meropenem and honey‐loaded Cs‐NPs were shown to considerably lower the produced biofilm when compared to free meropenem (C2 combination) (***p < 0.0001) (Figure 4). It has previously been shown that Cs vesicles interact electrostatically with negatively charged biofilms due to their cationic; the antibiotic may then be released into the biofilm structure (R). The findings also suggest that meropenem‐encapsulated Cs‐NPs (C5 combination) are more effective at removing biofilm than free meropenem (C2 combination) (**p < 0.01). Furthermore, the results demonstrate that Cs‐encapsulated honey is more efficient at eliminating biofilms than the C3 combination (free honey). As a result, Cs‐NPs are effective antimicrobial medication carriers for biofilm elimination. Encapsulation enabled more effective clearance of the biofilm in this study, with a 1‐ to 10‐fold lower MBIC of free meropenem (Figure 4).

sec.title: Meropenem‐honey Cs‐NPs reduce the transcription of biofilm‐associated genes
sec.p: The expression levels of biofilm‐associated genes (Bap, ompA, and pgaB) were examined using real‐time RT‐PCR tests to further validate the inhibitory impact of Cs‐encapsulated meropenem and honey combination NPs in S. aureus strains. All four isolates were treated with sub‐MIC concentrations of C1–C6, and the findings showed that Cs encapsulated with meropenem and honey had a substantial inhibitory impact on the expression of the ompA, pgaB, and Bap genes (***p < 0.00001). Figure 5 shows the results of gene expression compared to the 16SrRNA reference gene in positive biofilm strains before treatment with the drug and after treatment with the Cs‐encapsulated meropenem and honey. According to the findings, treatment with a different combination of Cs‐encapsulated meropenem caused the most significant decrease in the expression of genes ompA, pgaB, and Bap (p ≤ 0.05). Interestingly, among the various combinations, the C6 combination showed the best efficiency (***p < 0.00001).

sec.title: MTT assay
sec.p: The MTT assay was used to test the cytotoxicity of free and encapsulated meropenem against the HEK 293. The cells that were just exposed to media were utilized as a control, and their vitality was set to 100%. Seventy percent of the viable cells in control were established as the cytotoxic threshold. After 24 h, it was shown that Cs‐encapsulated meropenem and honey (C6 combination) showed minimal toxicity (cell survival over 70%) to HEK 293 cells at concentrations of 256 µM. However, free meropenem demonstrated toxicity at a dosage of 256 µM (Figure 6). The reduced toxicity may be due to the slower meropenem release of Cs than the free form. Only approximately half of the meropenem is released from Cs following a 24‐h interaction compared to the free form. As a result, the free form of meropenem (C2 combination) showed considerably more cytotoxicity than the Cs form. At 256 µM, cell viability was 95.33%, 95%, and 94% for the C3, C4, and C5 combination, respectively (Figure 6).

sec.title: Bactericidal effects of prepared NPs in vivo
sec.p: In immunocompetent mice, systemic infections were produced by injecting meropenem‐sensitive S. aureus intraperitoneally. Over 48 h, the survival of the control and treated mice was examined. All mice treated with C1 died, but mice given free meropenem died at 12/5%. However, the slight increase in animal survival was not statistically significant when compared to the C6 combination‐treated mice (p > 0.05). Compared to the other combinations, all animals treated with meropenem and honey‐loaded NPs dispersions survived for 48 h, indicating a considerable increase in survival rate (87.5%, p < 0.05). Also, the results show that the survival rate increased in mice treated with meropenem‐loaded Cs‐NPs compared to the free form of meropenem (50%). During the treatment period, there was a substantial change in body weight before and after challenging with S. aureus infection. The results show that the weights of mice in the group treated with C6 were close before and after the challenge. The animals’ physical appearance, food consumption, and excretion were all identical to those in the control groups. The results are mentioned in Table 8.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: The growing occurrence of MDR isolates makes treating infections caused by microbial resistance organisms complex, reducing the treatment choices available (Hassanen & Ragab, 2021). This was the situation with the S. aureus isolates collected in this investigation, where virtually all isolates were MDR (87.73%), in addition to the moderate percentage of MRSA found (35.33) in the limited number of MRSA treatment options available. The situation is made worse by the high prevalence of vancomycin resistance (70.96%), even though vancomycin is the antibiotic of choice for MRSA therapy. Furthermore, most of the isolates collected formed biofilms, making the treatment even more challenging. In modern medicine, developing a new practical approach to combat MRSA infection and substitute antibiotic therapy has become a pressing concern (Onanuga & Temedie, 2011). NPs have mainly been used in cancer therapy since their inception as medication delivery mechanics (Rybak et al., 2020). However, an expanding subgroup of studies focused on the antimicrobial aspect of this broad topic. The basic assumption of this study is that the development of novel meropenem‐honey‐Cs‐NPs was synthesized, and their anti‐infective characteristics were studied in this work. To determine the compatibility of the synthesized Cs‐NPs‐containing meropenem and honey for the desired purpose, many chemical methods were applied to evaluate them. The fabricated meropenem‐honey‐Cs‐NPs possessed high mono‐dispersity and a spherical shape, according to FESEM analysis. The FTIR data suggest that meropenem and honey successfully interact with the surface of the Cs‐NPs. A functional group comparable to its bulk counterpart in the FTIR spectra of NPs suggested effective encapsulation of meropenem and honey with Cs and the creation of meropenem and honey‐loaded Cs‐NPs. According to DLS analysis, the average particle size of meropenem and honey Cs‐NPs was roughly 266.2 nm, with a PDI of 0.118. The PDI is a number that ranges from 0 to 1. The closer this number is to zero, the better the particle size homogeneity (Van Duin & Paterson, 2016). For polymeric NPs, the ideal value is approximately 0 =–0.2; for drug release, this index should be below 0.4, and for other uses, up to 0.7 is appropriate and indicates particle size homogeneity (Gebreyohannes et al., 2019). As a result, the produced NPs with a PDI of 0.118 were shown to be appropriate for drug delivery. The DLS study yielded a hydrodynamic diameter of 266.2 nm for meropenem‐honey Cs‐NPs, which differed from that obtained by FESEM examination in a dry condition. The positive zeta potential of these NPs, which are firmly covered by water molecules while being dispersed in an aqueous solution for DLS analysis and show a sizeable hydrodynamic diameter compared to that obtained from FESEM analysis in a dry state, is attributed to the difference in particle size between DLS (262.2 nm) and FESEM (119.885 nm) (Cheng et al., 2019). Although smaller NPs have a higher encapsulation capacity due to their larger surface area, they also tend to aggregate easier when stored. The hydrodynamic size impacts various parameters, including loading efficiency, drug release kinetics, and NPs stability (Van Duin & Paterson, 2016). The synthesized meropenem‐honey Cs‐NPs have a zetapotential of +48 mV, indicating their outstanding stability and positivecharge, which makes them an efficient drug delivery technology antibiotics, also known as nanoantibiotics (Ghourchian et al., 2023).

The loading efficiency and controlled release of medication have a direct impact on its biological effectiveness as well as its potential for use in drug delivery (Cheng et al., 2019). The Cs‐NPs showed exceptional encapsulation efficiency and a long‐term release. Our results show that compared to previously produced nanocomposites, such as the Bovine Serum Albumin (BSA)‐loaded chitosan (Cs)‐tripolyphosphate (TPP) nanoparticles (NPs) with a loading efficacy of 60%, the meropenem‐honey Cs‐NPs demonstrated a greater loading efficiency (88.33%) (Ruseva et al., 2019). A hydrogen bond between the –OH group of meropenem and the ‐NH2 group of Cs, which aids in more significant trapping of meropenem into Cs‐NPs, may account for the high encapsulation effectiveness of Cs‐NPs (Ghasemzadeh et al., 2021). A similar finding was shown in meropenem‐loaded Cs‐NPs, where more than 71.5%–
76.3% of the drug was released after 4 hours, and no substantial amount was released beyond that (Hassanen & Ragab, 2021).

Staphylococcus aureus biofilm development has been linked to various nosocomial and chronic disorders linked to medical devices and surgical implants. It also results in the establishment of MDR bacteria, such as MRSA and vancomycin‐resistant S. aureus (Ghasemzadeh et al., 2021). The anti‐infection activity of generated meropenem and honey‐Cs‐NPs was demonstrated in vitro. Meropenem and honey‐Cs‐NPs were shown to have antibacterial effects on S. aureus growth and biofilm‐forming capabilities. While S. aureus was antibiotic‐resistant, it was highly susceptible to meropenem and honey encapsulated in Cs. Our results reveal that Cs encapsulated with honey (C4) and Cs encapsulated with meropenem (C5) have intense antibiofilm action compared to their free form. However, the antibiofilm efficacy was significantly increased when both were encapsulated with Cs. Furthermore, the lower MIC value for meropenem and honey‐Cs‐NPs compared to free meropenem or free honey indicates that meropenem and honey‐Cs‐NPs have more potent growth‐inhibitory effects, which is confidently linked to the presence of Cs. Cs derivatives have been shown to interact with microbial cell membranes, resulting in a loss of membrane integrity (Labruère et al., 2019). Cs‐NPs are also claimed to suppress S. aureus development by disrupting membranes and allowing metabolites to leak out. According to Table 7, the free Cs, free meropenem, and free honey had a lower bactericidal effect and selective pressure against S. aureus at the MIC level. However, it significantly impacted S. aureus in the biofilm formation state. In acceptable quantities, encapsulated Cs containing meropenem and honey have been proven harmless in HEK‐293 cells. The suggested daily dose of these NPs is 1–256 µM, according to reports. Meanwhile, free meropenem (C2 combination) is nontoxic at low doses and only hazardous at higher concentrations. NPs produced with C1, C3, C4, and C5 combinations in various dosages were similarly shown to be non‐toxic. Because of the nontoxic nature of these components, Cs‐NPs may be used in biomedical activities. Based on the findings of this study, it can be concluded that encapsulating meropenem and honey in Cs nanogels improves its antibacterial capabilities while allowing for controlled drug delivery and release. To assess antibiofilm activity, the expression of the biofilm genes OmpA, Bap, and pgaB was evaluated in NPs at MBIC concentrations. The results revealed that meropenem and honey‐based Cs‐NPs caused the most significant reduction in gene expression in all four bacterium isolates, suggesting that meropenem and honey‐based Cs‐NPs interact with transcription factors, inhibiting gene expression. The study's final goal was to examine the non‐toxicity of meropenem and honey‐based Cs nanogels in a septic mouse model of S. aureus. The results revealed a significant increase in survival and body weight compared to the animals given the free antibiotic.

Studies conducted in 2016 by Qi et al. (2016) show a direct link between antibiotic resistance, biofilm development, and biofilm‐specific resistance statistically in A. baumannii. Siddhardha et al. (2020) have indicated that loading chrysin onto Cs‐TPP NPs increased the antibiofilm action of chrysin against S. aureus, with a significant loading capacity. In both in vitro and in vivo trials, another finding demonstrated a synergistic antibacterial/antibiofilm action of hydrogen peroxide (HP) and antimicrobial peptide. In mouse models, the HP‐releasing Cs hydrogels have shown the ability to prevent bacterial biofilm‐related infections and improve wound healing. These findings show that HP‐releasing Cs hydrogels might be a better platform for removing bacterial biofilms without using antibiotics to treat persistent MRSA wound infections, enhancing human health (Fasiku et al., 2021). The antibacterial properties of Cs‐NPs, meropenem‐free drugs, free honey, and meropenem‐honey‐based Cs nanogels were investigated using the suitable diffusion method in this study. The results revealed that the meropenem‐honey‐based Cs nanogels with the largest diameter of growth inhibition in all four MDR genera had the best growth inhibition. The findings of this study, like those of earlier investigations, show that when antibacterial drugs are combined with Cs‐NPs, their characteristics improve. Studies conducted show that the bactericidal activity of meropenem in combination with Cs nanogels increases in mouse models of systemic infection with S. aureus. In addition, compared to animals given the free drug, the meropenem‐loaded NPs resulted in improved survival rates and excellent bacterial clearance (i.e., 99%). As a result, meropenem and honey Cs‐NPs might be evaluated as potential therapeutic strategies for preventing S. aureus biofilm development. The nanocomposites might be used to build antibiofilm coatings in the future. Cs has remarkable qualities that make it very versatile and applicable in many fields. However, it is important to note that Cs also has certain limitations. Its limited solubility in water and most organic solvents restricts its applicability in several industries. Furthermore, Cs NPs suffer from constraints such as cytotoxicity, degradability, and poor mechanical qualities. However, these challenges may be addressed by the process of cross‐linking or stabilizing such materials (Asadipour et al., 2023).

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: In conclusion, Cs, a pharmacological system based on a polymer acetylated from oral chitin that separates from the shrimp's hard shell, has shown promise in enhancing the antibacterial effects of medical or natural antibacterial compounds. This study displayed the improved antibiofilm activity of meropenem and honey against multidrug resistant S. aureus when loaded onto Cs NPs, with a profound loading capacity. The NPs developed in this study had a small particle size, which might promote drug penetration into bacterial cells and antibacterial effectiveness. As a result, encapsulating meropenem and honey in Cs nanogels not only improves their antibacterial and antibiofilm properties but also reduces their cytotoxic properties and increases the efficiency of meropenem based on characteristics such as targeted binding to bacterial levels and drug‐controlled release. Because of their biocompatibility and antibacterial activity, Cs NPs are expected to be widely used as a medical carrier for antimicrobial drugs. Finally, the usage of meropenem and honey‐based Cs NPs in the pharmaceutical business might be described as a novel strategy.
